rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to reveal the full elution window and avoid truncation while giving useful spacing information across all 6 compounds. This should show whether peaks are unretained early, retained into the hold, or distributed across the gradient so later runs can tighten the window and adjust slope.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the objective is now to cut retention time while keeping every peak inside the gradient. The observed peaks span roughly phi_e about 0.18 to 0.68, so a trimmed window with a shorter gradient should greatly reduce t_last while still leaving margin at both ends.

We already have the maximum CRF, so now map the speed limit by shortening the gradient one step while keeping the same successful window and temperature. This tests whether the closest pair still stays above 1.5 as we push for an even faster method.

The same window remains comfortably over-resolved at 6 minutes, with the first pair still the limiting one, so the next efficient move is to shorten tG again. This brackets the minimum usable gradient time before resolution begins to approach the 1.5 threshold.

At 4 minutes the worst pair is still well above 1.5, so we should test the shortest allowed gradient on the same successful window. This directly checks whether the method can be pushed to the minimum run time without sacrificing full-credit resolution.

The 2-minute run showed the first pair is the sole limit, so the best lever is to give the earliest peaks more starting retention by lowering phi0 while keeping the successful short gradient. This may improve the 1/2 separation and could open room to shorten further later.

Lowering phi0 improved the critical first pair at 4 minutes, so the next step is to combine that lower start with the 2-minute gradient that previously failed. This directly tests whether extra early retention is enough to recover full resolution at the shortest gradient.

The 2-minute gradients fail only on pair 1/2, suggesting this pair is not rescued by slope or lower phi0 and may need a selectivity change. A 5 C drop is a modest, low-risk way to test whether temperature improves that critical early pair while keeping the currently fastest fully resolved window.

Lowering temperature materially improved the critical 1/2 pair at 4 minutes, so the key next test is whether that selectivity gain is enough to make the 2-minute gradient fully resolved. This is the most direct route to a faster all-pairs-above-1.5 method.

At 2 minutes and 35 C only pair 1/2 is slightly below threshold, and narrowing the gradient window should reduce steepness enough to help that pair without materially hurting runtime. Bringing phi1 down one step is the cleanest slope adjustment because the last peak is still very early.

We now have a fully resolved 2-minute method, so the remaining optimization is to trim the window further until a pair approaches the limit. Lowering phi1 one more step should further reduce gradient steepness and may improve the critical 1/2 pair while checking whether the late compound still stays comfortably inside the gradient/hold.

With phi1 = 0.70 the method is fully resolved and the critical pair is only just above threshold, so a useful next test is whether shifting the whole 2-minute window slightly later shortens the run while preserving acceptable early-pair resolution. This probes whether the current low phi0 is more conservative than necessary.

The shifted 0.20–0.70 window stayed fully resolved and gave the shortest fully resolved runtime so far, so the next move is to raise phi1 one step to see if the last peak can be pulled even earlier while keeping pair 1/2 above 1.5. This tests whether 0.70 is already the upper edge or whether there is still headroom for a faster 2-minute method.

The current best practical region is the 2-minute, 35 C method with pair 1/2 sitting just above threshold, so the next efficient boundary test is to raise phi0 one step to see if runtime can be trimmed further without losing that pair. This directly probes how far we can push the earliest peaks toward the dead-time limit before resolution breaks.

At phi0 = 0.25 the first peak is still retained and the critical pair remains above 1.5, so one more step higher in phi0 is the right edge test for an even more aggressive 2-minute method. This checks whether we can further compress the early end without crossing into effectively unretained behavior or losing the 1/2 separation.

phi0 = 0.30 proved too aggressive for the first pair, so keep the successful phi0 = 0.25 and test whether a one-step higher phi1 can pull the last peak earlier without dropping the critical 1/2 pair below 1.5. This is the most informative remaining edge test around the fastest fully resolved region.

The 0.25–0.80 window is the fastest fully resolved method so far but sits exactly on the resolution cutoff for pair 1/2, so lowering phi0 one step should add a small safety margin while likely keeping the last peak very early. This tests whether we can retain essentially the same speed with a more robust separation.

The 0.25–0.80 method is currently the fastest fully resolved option, and pair 1/2 is exactly at the threshold, so one final phi1 increase cleanly tests whether any more speed is available. This is the relevant edge probe because the late peaks should move earlier while the first pair will reveal immediately if the window has become too steep.

We have likely found the speed edge in composition space at 35 C, with 0.25–0.80 just meeting the cutoff, so a 5 C drop is the most promising way to gain selectivity margin on pair 1/2 while preserving the very fast 2-minute window. This tests whether the same fast method can be made more robust, or potentially support an even more aggressive window later.

Lowering to 30 C gave a useful selectivity cushion on the critical first pair while keeping the 2-minute method very fast, so the next boundary test is to revisit phi1 = 0.85 under this more favorable temperature. This checks whether the faster late elution from a higher phi1 can now be achieved without dropping pair 1/2 below 1.5.

At 30 C the 0.25–0.85 method remains fully resolved with useful margin on the critical pair, so one more increase in phi1 is the logical final speed test. This probes whether the last peak can be brought even earlier while keeping pair 1/2 above the 1.5 cutoff.

The 0.25–0.90, 2-minute, 30 C method is still fully resolved with pair 1/2 just above threshold, so one last increase in phi1 is the natural edge test for the fastest possible fully resolved method. If resolution holds, this should further shorten the last peak and define the practical limit.

We now know phi1 = 0.90 at 30 C is fully resolved while 0.95 is too steep, so the remaining way to trim the window is to raise phi0 one step and see whether the faster early end still keeps pair 1/2 above 1.5. This probes whether a narrower, shifted-high window can match or beat the current fastest successful method.

The 0.30–0.90 window at 30 C is fully resolved with slightly more margin than 0.25–0.90, so it is worth one final push to phi1 = 0.95 from this stronger starting point. This directly tests whether the shifted-high window can reach an even faster fully resolved boundary than the 0.25 series.

The 0.30–0.95, 2-minute, 30 C method is now the fastest fully resolved point and still has a small margin on the critical first pair, so the final injection should test one last increase in phi0. This is the remaining plausible route to an even faster fully resolved boundary, while the first two peaks will immediately show if we have gone too far.
